title: Value types and reference types
body: Every C# type is either a value type or a reference type. Structs (including `int`, `double`, `bool`, `DateTime`) and enums are value types: a variable of a value type directly contains the value, and assignment copies it. Classes, arrays, strings, delegates and records declared with `record class` are reference types: a variable holds a reference to an object on the managed heap, and assignment copies the reference, not the object.

After `var b = a;` with a struct, `a` and `b` are independent: changing `b.X` leaves `a.X` alone. With a class, both variables refer to the same object, so a change through one name is visible through the other. This aliasing is the single most important thing to predict when reading C#.

Passing an argument copies the variable's contents too. A method that receives a class reference can mutate the shared object, but assigning a new object to its parameter only changes the method's local copy of the reference. To replace the caller's variable itself, the parameter must be `ref`.

Value types are not always on the stack: a struct field inside a class lives inside that object on the heap, and an array of structs stores the structs inline. Think in terms of copy semantics, not storage location. Small, immutable structs (marked `readonly struct`) are cheap to copy and avoid accidental mutation of a copy.

A classic bug is mutating a copy: `list[0].X = 5` on a `List<MutablePoint>` struct is a compile error (CS1612) because the indexer returns a copy. Before mutating, check whether the expression gives you the original storage or a copy, and prefer immutable structs so the question rarely matters.

challenge: Declare a readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount) and a method Add that returns a new Money. Show that adding to a copy leaves the original unchanged.
question: After `var b = a;` where `a` is a class instance, what does changing `b.Name` do?
correct: Changes the object that a also refers to
wrong: Is rejected because a and b alias
reasoning: Class assignment copies the reference, so both variables name the same object.
